props.title: Mikey and Nicky
props.initialSlug: Two mob friends, one marked for death, one night

sections.content: **Mikey and Nicky (1976)** (1976) represents one of the most intense examinations of male friendship ever captured on film. Director Elaine May spent over a year editing 1.4 million feet of footage to craft this raw, documentary-like portrait of betrayal. Like a grittier companion piece to Mean Streets (1973), the film follows two small-time mobsters through a long, desperate night in Philadelphia. Peter Falk and John Cassavetes deliver career-defining performances, drawing on their real-life friendship to create an authenticity that bleeds through every scene.

sections.content: The film's production was notoriously difficult, with May shooting over 1.4 million feet of film (nearly three times what was shot for **Gone with the Wind** (1939)). She insisted on multiple takes and angles, often running three cameras simultaneously to capture the electric unpredictability between Falk and Cassavetes. This approach nearly bankrupted Paramount but resulted in an unmatched immediacy that influenced later films like **Thief** (1981) and **At Close Range** (1986).

May's direction subverts typical gangster film tropes by focusing on the psychological warfare between two lifelong friends rather than traditional mob movie violence. The result feels more like **In the Company of Men** (1997) than **The Godfather** (1972), examining toxic masculinity and betrayal through an intimate lens. The film's influence can be seen in later works like **The Friends of Eddie Coyle** (1973) and **Donnie Brasco** (1997). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of the Anti-Gangster Film

sections.content: **Mikey and Nicky** helped establish a new subset of crime films that prioritized character study over action. This approach influenced works like **Miller's Crossing** (1990) and **The Long Good Friday** (1980), where the psychological tension between characters drives the narrative. May's film strips away glamour to show the paranoid, pathetic reality of low-level criminals, setting a template for later works like **Buffalo '66** (1998) and **Killing Them Softly** (2012).
